TomTom's New Route Runs Through AI: Discovery Event Reveals Strategic Pivot

At its TomTom Discovery Event in Amsterdam, the company revealed a fundamental strategic repositioning: maps are no longer primarily for guiding people, but for navigating AI and machines, with Orbis serving as a spatial knowledge layer for autonomous driving and enterprise AI agents.

Key takeaways
  • TomTom is shifting from 40 years of helping humans understand the physical world to helping intelligent systems and AI understand and move within it
  • CEO Mike Schoofs aims to provide the critical safety map layer for more than half of all new European cars by 2030
  • The company has transitioned from hardware (navigation devices with ~40% margins) to pure software (gross margins heading toward 90%)
  • Orbis Maps serves as "ground truth" — a uniform, verified reference reality combining OpenStreetMap, Overture Maps, TomTom's own data, and vehicle sensor data
  • The platform uses more than 5 billion data points to continuously enrich and verify the map, with 2.8 trillion kilometres of worldwide distance data stored
  • TomTom has made Orbis APIs and an MCP server available for AI agents to access spatial intelligence
  • Location intelligence is identified as a double-digit growth market, with 70-80% of enterprise data containing a spatial component

This Little-Known Google Maps Setting Saves Your Battery and Mobile Data

Google Maps' offline maps feature can save both battery and mobile data, but a hidden default setting silently updates downloaded maps over cellular data without user confirmation — here's how to fix it.

Key takeaways
  • GPS navigation is one of the most battery-intensive tasks on a smartphone, simultaneously using GPS, screen, CPU, and mobile data
  • Google Maps' offline maps feature allows pre-downloading detailed maps to navigate without a network connection
  • Once downloaded, the app no longer needs to constantly request mobile data to display streets and points of interest
  • A hidden default setting automatically updates offline maps over both Wi-Fi and cellular data without asking for confirmation
  • The update process runs in the background with no notification or visible indication
  • Disabling "Automatically update offline maps" and "Automatically download recommended maps" prevents unwanted data consumption
  • Restricting offline map updates to Wi-Fi only further protects mobile data allowances

Could the World Map Change? What the UN's New Move Means for India

UN General Assembly Votes to Promote Equal Earth Projection for More Accurate World Maps

The UN General Assembly voted 164-1 to promote equal-area map projections like Equal Earth, encouraging governments, schools, and tech companies to represent continents at their true relative sizes rather than the distorted Mercator view used since the 16th century.

Key takeaways
  • The UN General Assembly voted on September 4, 2026, with 164 in favor, 1 against, and 6 abstentions to promote equal-area world map projections
  • The resolution was sponsored by Togo and encourages governments, educational institutions, international organizations, and technology companies to adopt equal-area projections
  • The 2018 Equal Earth projection is identified as an example of a map that accurately represents continental scale
  • The resolution does not formally replace or prohibit the Mercator projection, which has been used since the 16th century
  • It calls for education about the limitations of representing Earth's curved surface on a two-dimensional map
  • The resolution is non-binding but could influence cartographic standards in education and digital mapping

Why the UN's New World Map Won't Change Google Maps Anytime Soon

The UN's adoption of the Equal Earth projection resolution won't change Google Maps because the app's tiling system depends on Mercator's angle-preserving properties, and the resolution is nonbinding.

Key takeaways
  • The UN resolution passed with 164 votes in favour, 1 against (US), and 6 abstentions, but is nonbinding
  • France announced it will switch official maps from Mercator to Eckert IV projection
  • Google Maps uses a square-tile system since 2005 that requires Mercator's angle-preserving properties at all zoom levels
  • Equal Earth and Eckert IV preserve surface areas but sacrifice angular accuracy, making them incompatible with current tile-based mapping infrastructure
  • Togo plans to meet with Google, the African Union, and UNESCO within six months to discuss practical implementation

What Different World Maps Get Right — and What They Get Wrong

The BBC provides a comparative analysis of the world's most prominent map projections — Mercator, Equal Earth, and Peters — explaining the trade-offs between area accuracy, shape fidelity, and navigational utility.

Key takeaways
  • No flat map can perfectly represent a spherical Earth; every projection sacrifices something
  • Mercator preserves compass bearings but massively distorts area, making Africa look Greenland-sized
  • Equal Earth, adopted by the UN, preserves area accuracy but cannot be used for navigation
  • The Peters projection (1973) also preserves area but severely distorts shapes of landmasses
  • Critics argue Mercator's distortions have psychological effects, shaping how regions are perceived politically and economically

The Agent Drafts, a Human Approves: Inside State of the Map US 2026

State of the Map US 2026 in Madison, Wisconsin revealed three trends reshaping geospatial engineering: serverless map stacks replacing databases and tile servers with columnar files on object storage, AI agents drafting map data at industrial volume, and the deliberate human curation of sidewalk-level map data.

Key takeaways
  • Serverless map pipelines are shedding traditional databases and tile servers in favor of columnar files on object storage with parallel build steps
  • AI agents are now drafting map data at industrial volume — from dashcam detections and satellite-derived geometry to automated validation of OSM contributions
  • Sean Gorman's talk proposed restructuring OpenStreetMap tiles for AI consumption: embeddings, not pixels, as models now consume maps alongside humans
  • Jeremy Herzog demonstrated restructuring the HIFLD critical infrastructure dataset for AI system consumption ("How We Prepared HIFLD for the Singularity")
  • Sidewalks, crossings, and curbs — the fastest-growing part of the map — remain hand-drawn by the community, a deliberate choice the OSM community defends
  • The guiding principle across all three trends: "the agent drafts, a human approves" — AI proposes, humans curate
